Title: The Sun Never Set (Part 1 of 10): Before the Empire Had a Name, 1497–1660

Summary: The British Empire did not begin with a grand plan. It began with fishing fleets, pirates licensed by the Crown, the conquest of Ireland, and a trading company that was tiny next to its Dutch rivals. This first post covers 1497 to 1660 and lines up England's first footholds against what the Mughals, Ottomans, Ming and Tokugawa were doing at the same moment.

---

## About this series

This is a ten-part timeline of the British Empire from its first Atlantic voyages to the handover of Hong Kong in 1997 and the loose ends that remain. The goal is not to retell every battle. It is to put events side by side so you can see what was happening **at the same time** in different parts of the world, because that is where most of us have blind spots. Most people know about 1776 and 1857. Fewer know that the British were fighting the Maratha Confederacy in India while the American Revolution was still going on.

Each post has three kinds of tables:

- **Main timeline**: what Britain and its empire were doing.
- **Meanwhile**: world events in the same years, related or not.
- **Resistance**: risings, mutinies and wars fought against British rule.

A note on names: before 1707 there was no "Britain" as a state. England (with Wales) and Scotland were separate kingdoms sharing a king after 1603. I say "English" for this period and "British" afterwards. Dates are given as historians usually give them; where a date or number is disputed, I flag it.

The series:

1. Before the Empire Had a Name, 1497–1660 (this post)
2. Sugar, Slavery and Company Men, 1660–1756
3. The First Global War, 1756–1783
4. Losing America, Gaining the World, 1783–1815
5. Free Trade, Opium and Abolition, 1815–1856
6. Rebellion and the Crown, 1857–1879
7. The Scramble and the Summit, 1880–1913
8. Total War and the First Cracks, 1914–1938
9. The Fall Begins, 1939–1959
10. Winds of Change to the Last Flag, 1960–1997 and After

## The starting position

In 1500 England was a small, mid-ranking kingdom on the edge of Europe. Portugal and Spain had a head start of nearly a century. Spain was pulling silver out of the Americas, Portugal controlled the sea route to Asia, and in 1494 the Treaty of Tordesillas had split the non-European world between the two of them on paper. England's early "empire" was mostly ambition, piracy, and Ireland.

## Main timeline: voyages, privateers and plantations (1497–1603)

| Year | What happened | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| 1497 | John Cabot, a Venetian sailing for Henry VII, reaches North America (probably Newfoundland or Cape Breton; the exact landfall is disputed) | Later used as the basis for English claims in North America |
| 1534 | Henry VIII breaks with Rome | Protestant England now sees Catholic Spain as a religious as well as commercial rival |
| 1541 | Henry VIII declared King of Ireland | Turns a loose lordship into a claim to full rule |
| 1556–1558 | First "plantation" of Laois and Offaly in Ireland | The model of confiscating land and settling loyal colonists, later used across the Atlantic |
| 1562–1569 | John Hawkins makes the first English slaving voyages, taking Africans from West Africa to sell in the Spanish Caribbean | England's entry into the transatlantic slave trade |
| 1577–1580 | Francis Drake sails around the world, raiding Spanish ships and ports | Privateering becomes state policy; Elizabeth I shares the profits |
| 1583 | Humphrey Gilbert claims Newfoundland for England | Often called the first formal English overseas claim; Gilbert drowned on the way home |
| 1585–1590 | Roanoke colonies (in today's North Carolina); the 1587 settlers vanish | The "Lost Colony"; the first attempts fail |
| 1586 | Plantation of Munster begins after the Desmond Rebellions | Large-scale settlement of English colonists in southern Ireland |
| 1588 | Spanish Armada defeated | Not the end of Spanish power, but a huge boost to English naval confidence |
| 1600 | East India Company (EIC) chartered on 31 December | Starts as a small trading venture; becomes the most powerful company in history |
| 1603 | James VI of Scotland becomes James I of England (Union of the Crowns) | One king, two kingdoms; the word "Britain" starts to be used |

## Main timeline: colonies and companies (1603–1660)

| Year | What happened | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| 1607 | Jamestown, Virginia founded | First permanent English settlement in the Americas; most of the first settlers died within a few years |
| 1607 | Flight of the Earls: Ulster's Gaelic lords leave Ireland | Opens the way for the Plantation of Ulster |
| 1609 | Plantation of Ulster begins | English and Scottish Protestants settled on confiscated land; its legacy runs into the 20th century |
| 1612 | Bermuda settled (after the 1609 wreck of the Sea Venture) | One of the oldest surviving British territories today |
| 1612–1613 | EIC defeats the Portuguese at Swally, near Surat, and opens a trading post (factory) at Surat | First foothold in Mughal India |
| 1615–1619 | Sir Thomas Roe is ambassador to the Mughal emperor Jahangir | England arrives as a minor petitioner at a vastly richer court |
| 1619 | First recorded enslaved Africans arrive in Virginia | Start of slavery in English North America |
| 1620 | Mayflower lands; Plymouth Colony founded | Puritan New England begins |
| 1622 | Powhatan Confederacy attacks Virginia settlements, killing about a quarter of the colonists | One of the first major Indigenous wars against English colonisation |
| 1623 | Amboyna massacre: the Dutch execute English EIC men in the Spice Islands | England is pushed out of the Indonesian spice trade and refocuses on India |
| 1624 | St Kitts settled | First English Caribbean colony |
| 1627 | Barbados settled | Becomes the first great English sugar and slave colony |
| 1630 | Massachusetts Bay Colony founded | Large Puritan migration in the 1630s |
| 1636–1638 | Pequot War in New England | Pequot nation nearly destroyed; survivors enslaved or dispersed |
| 1639–1640 | EIC builds Fort St George at Madras (Chennai) | First fortified English base in India |
| 1641 | Irish Rebellion; Catholic Irish rise against Protestant settlers | Thousands of settlers killed; reports were exaggerated in England and used to justify revenge |
| 1642–1651 | English Civil Wars (part of the wider Wars of the Three Kingdoms) | Colonies split between Royalist and Parliament sides |
| 1649 | Charles I executed; Cromwell invades Ireland (Drogheda and Wexford massacres) | Cromwellian conquest and land confiscation transfer most Irish land to Protestant ownership |
| 1651 | First Navigation Act | Colonial trade must use English ships; the legal backbone of a mercantile empire |
| 1652–1654 | First Anglo-Dutch War | The first of three wars over sea trade |
| 1655 | Jamaica taken from Spain in Cromwell's "Western Design" | The intended target, Hispaniola, failed; Jamaica becomes the biggest sugar colony |
| 1660 | Restoration of Charles II | The start of a much more organised imperial state |

## Meanwhile: the rest of the world (1492–1660)

This is the key point of the early period. The English were latecomers next to empires far richer than them.

| Years | Event | Region |
|---|---|---|
| 1492 | Columbus reaches the Caribbean; Granada falls to Castile | Americas and Spain |
| 1498 | Vasco da Gama reaches India by sea | Indian Ocean |
| 1517 | Luther's 95 Theses; Ottomans conquer Mamluk Egypt | Europe and Middle East |
| 1519–1521 | Cortés and his Indigenous allies bring down the Aztec Empire | Mexico |
| 1526 | Babur wins at Panipat and founds the Mughal Empire | India |
| 1529 | Ottoman siege of Vienna | Central Europe |
| 1532–1533 | Pizarro captures and kills the Inca emperor Atahualpa | Peru |
| 1545 | Silver discovered at Potosí | Bolivia; Spanish silver floods the world economy and much of it flows to Ming China |
| 1556–1605 | Reign of Akbar; the Mughal Empire becomes one of the richest states on earth | India |
| 1571 | Battle of Lepanto; Spain founds Manila | Mediterranean and Philippines |
| 1592–1598 | Japanese invasions of Korea under Hideyoshi | East Asia |
| 1602 | Dutch East India Company (VOC) founded, far better funded than the English EIC | Netherlands |
| 1603 | Tokugawa shogunate begins | Japan |
| 1608 | Quebec founded by the French | North America |
| 1616 | Deaths of Shakespeare and Cervantes (within days of each other, though in different calendars) | Europe |
| 1618–1648 | Thirty Years' War devastates central Europe | Europe |
| 1632–1653 | Taj Mahal built under Shah Jahan | India |
| 1639 | Japan restricts European contact (sakoku); only the Dutch may trade, at Nagasaki | Japan |
| 1644 | Ming dynasty falls; Qing (Manchu) rule begins | China |
| 1648 | Peace of Westphalia | Europe |
| 1652 | Dutch found a station at the Cape of Good Hope | Southern Africa; Britain will take it 150 years later |

## Resistance: early wars against English expansion

| Years | Who | Against what | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1569–1573, 1579–1583 | Desmond Rebellions (Munster, Ireland) | Tudor expansion | Crushed; famine followed; Munster plantation |
| 1593–1603 | Nine Years' War, led by Hugh O'Neill | Tudor conquest of Ulster | Irish and Spanish defeated at Kinsale (1601); Ulster opened to plantation |
| 1610–1614 | First Anglo-Powhatan War | Jamestown settlers | Ended partly through the marriage of Pocahontas and John Rolfe |
| 1622 and 1644 | Powhatan attacks led by Opechancanough | Expansion of Virginia tobacco farms | Powhatan power broken by 1646 |
| 1636–1638 | Pequot War | New England settlers | Pequot defeated; Mystic massacre (1637) |
| 1641–1653 | Irish Confederate Wars | Protestant settlement and English rule | Ended by Cromwell's conquest |

## Things that happened at the same time

- **1600–1602.** The English EIC was chartered just over a year before the Dutch VOC, but the VOC started with roughly ten times the capital. For most of the 17th century the English were the junior player in Asia.
- **1607.** Jamestown was founded in the same year that Ulster's Gaelic lords fled Ireland. The same generation of English adventurers and investors were involved in both, and settlers in Virginia were sometimes compared with planters in Ulster.
- **1619–1620.** The first enslaved Africans reached Virginia one year before the Mayflower. Both are "founding" stories of English America.
- **1632–1653.** While the Taj Mahal was being built, English traders in India were running a few fortified warehouses and depended on Mughal permission to trade.
- **1644–1649.** The Ming dynasty fell to the Manchus in the same decade that England fell into civil war and executed its king.

## Sources and flags

- John Darwin, *Unfinished Empire: The Global Expansion of Britain* (2012).
- Nicholas Canny (ed.), *The Oxford History of the British Empire, Volume I: The Origins of Empire* (1998).
- William Dalrymple, *The Anarchy: The Relentless Rise of the East India Company* (2019), on the EIC's beginnings.
- Encyclopaedia Britannica, "British Empire": https://www.britannica.com/place/British-Empire
- **Flag:** Cabot's exact landfall in 1497 is unknown. The VOC versus EIC capital comparison is a commonly cited rough ratio, not an exact figure. Casualty figures for the 1641 rebellion and Cromwell's campaign in Ireland are heavily disputed and I have not given numbers for that reason.
